entry.evidence: the Mw 6.1 Pasaman earthquake was not located along any of its recognized segments

steps.action: The authors take as their case the live Mw 6.1 Pasaman mainshock of 25 February 2022 and its Mw 5.1 foreshock, recorded by the permanent BMKG network.
steps.quote: On February 25th, 2022, an Mw 6.1 earthquake occurred at 01:39 UTC to the west of Pasaman

steps.action: They cite earlier temporary-array seismicity near the target area, including a 5-12 km deep cluster close to the 2022 event.
steps.quote: detected several small earthquake clusters between April 2008 and February 2009 using a dense local network

steps.action: They note that the event lies off every recognized Great Sumatran Fault segment and ask which fault ruptured.
steps.quote: the Mw 6.1 Pasaman earthquake was not located along any of its recognized segments

steps.action: They state two rivals: an undiscovered segment of the Great Sumatran Fault, or a different, also unknown fault.
steps.quote: whether a previously undiscovered segment of the Great Sumatran Fault ruptured, or whether a different – but also unknown – fault was responsible

steps.action: They assemble 2798 P and 1067 S arrival times for 201 events (M 1.4-6.1) from 16 BMKG stations, 25 February to 8 March 2022.
steps.quote: A total of 201 earthquakes with a magnitude range of M 1.4 to M 6.1 were detected

steps.action: They relocate the foreshock, mainshock and 196 aftershocks with double-difference HypoDD in a 1-D CRUST 1.0 velocity model, starting from BMKG LocSAT/IASP91 locations; five events above the surface are discarded.
steps.quote: We relocated a foreshock, a mainshock, and 196 aftershocks related to the 2021 Pasaman earthquake

steps.action: Methods: they chose the HypoDD parameters (40 km separation, 60 neighbours, 10 links, 160 km station distance) after testing value combinations.
steps.quote: These input parameter selections are made following extensive testing to determine the combination of values that produced the best results

steps.action: They compare the relocations with the initial BMKG catalogue locations, which had fixed depths, and report lower travel-time residuals after relocation (Fig. S1).
steps.quote: The travel-time residuals after HypoDD relocation clearly decrease (see supplementary Fig. S1)

steps.action: They rerun the same workflow with the 1-D velocity model of Weller et al. (2012) and get a nearly identical pattern with a slightly shallower centroid (Fig. S2).
steps.quote: The results (see Fig. S2) show a nearly identical pattern of events, but with a slight shallowing of the cluster centroid.

steps.action: They estimate location uncertainty with a 200-iteration bootstrap of residuals and report average mislocations of 0.5 km horizontally and 0.8 km vertically, with a maximum of 10 km in depth.
steps.quote: reveal average horizontal and vertical mislocations of 0.5 km and 0.8 km respectively

steps.action: They compare the relocated sequence with mapped faults: a ~20 km NW-SE band parallel to the Great Sumatran Fault, lying between the Talamau and Angkola faults rather than on any mapped fault.
steps.quote: The distribution of relocated aftershocks extends ~20 km from the northwest to the southeast in a band that is parallel to the Great Sumatran fault

steps.action: They keep the interpretation that the band is a newly identified fault segment and name it the Kajai Fault.
steps.quote: [...] that it is a newly identified segment, which we call the Kajai Fault

steps.action: They check the inferred fault against independent surface morphology: a NW-SE trace aligned with the hypocentre elongation (Fig. S4).
steps.quote: The existence of the Kajai Fault is also supported by the surface morphology (Fig. S4).

steps.action: They set the fault orientation beside published shear-wave-splitting results that show NW-SE fast axes near the fault.
steps.quote: the fast axis orientation of anisotropy is NW-SE, parallel to the Great Sumatran fault

steps.action: They refine the interpretation: the Kajai Fault may be an active conjugate fault of the Great Sumatran Fault.
steps.quote: may also be considered a conjugate fault of the Great Sumatran fault that is currently active

steps.action: They invert regional waveforms (Kiwi Tools, amplitude spectra, 0.01-0.07/0.08 Hz, IASP91) for moment tensors of the foreshock, mainshock and two Mw 5.0 aftershocks; misfits are below 0.45 and solutions about 89% double-couple.
steps.quote: Our moment tensor inversion recovers solutions that are nearly 89% double-couple on average

steps.action: They vary the upper filter frequency (0.15 Hz, 1.5 Hz); the double-couple percentage falls to 75% and about 50% (Fig. S8), which supports the low-frequency choice.
steps.quote: using an upper frequency of 0.15 Hz produces solutions that are 75% double couple

steps.action: They choose the SW-dipping right-lateral nodal plane (strike N132E, dip 72SW) as the fault plane, using the aftershock distribution, and reject the conjugate nodal plane.
steps.quote: Based on the aftershock distribution, the actual fault plane is interpreted to be the nodal plane that corresponds to the right-lateral fault

steps.action: They run a finite-fault inversion of teleseismic body and surface waves (wavelet domain, simulated annealing, 42 subfaults, CRUST1.0/PREM Green's functions). The result: Mw 6.14, a single compact asperity 2-11 km deep and ~14 x 9 km, peak slip 53 cm, up-dip rupture at ~1.5 km/s.
steps.quote: The inverted rupture model indicates a single, compact asperity with a depth range of 2–11 km

steps.action: They check the rupture extent from the teleseismic finite-fault model against the independently located aftershock distribution.
steps.quote: The rupture extent obtained from finite-fault modelling is consistent with the aftershock distribution.

steps.action: They estimate the static stress drop over the asperity (circular-rupture assumption) at about 1.9 MPa and relate the low value to high aftershock productivity.
steps.quote: over the asperity is about 1.9 MPa

steps.action: They list rival nucleation models for the foreshock and the ~2 s nucleation phase (stochastic triggering, deterministic pre-slip, progressive localization) and do not decide among them.
steps.quote: other conceptual models that explain the nucleation mechanism of the mainshock are also possible

steps.action: They compute the Coulomb static stress change from the inverted slip with AutoCoulomb (friction 0.4) on receiver faults with the mainshock geometry (Fig. 7).
steps.quote: Static stress changes caused by the Mw 6.1 mainshock (Fig. 7) reveal areas of increased stress

steps.action: They compare the stress-increase lobes with the aftershock distribution: increases to the NW and SE match the aftershocks, while high stress on the Angkola and Sumpur segments has no aftershocks.
steps.quote: this stress then transferred to the northwest and southeast and caused aftershocks

steps.action: They conclude that the sequence was caused by slip on the newly identified ~20 km dextral strike-slip Kajai Fault, part of the Great Sumatran Fault network, and flag possible increased hazard on Angkola and Sumpur pending further work.
steps.quote: The Mw 6.1 Pasaman earthquakes were caused by slip along the newly identified and ~ 20 km long dextral strike-slip Kajai fault

tree.answer: A destructive Mw 6.1 earthquake located off all mapped Great Sumatran Fault segments
No; the causative fault is inferred from relocated hypocentres and source inversions
Identify the fault that ruptured and characterize the rupture and stress changes
Yes: an undiscovered Great Sumatran Fault segment versus a different unknown fault; later also a conjugate-fault reading
Not stated; no prediction is given that would separate the two rivals
Conditions found: one live earthquake sequence recorded by a permanent network

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: No; a single sequence, with only cited earlier seismicity nearby
Partly: velocity-model swap, parameter tests, bootstrap, filter-band test, surface morphology
Kept: the Kajai Fault, a new segment within the Great Sumatran Fault network

end.claim: The 2022 Pasaman sequence ruptured a previously unidentified ~20 km dextral strike-slip fault (Kajai Fault, strike N132E, dip 72SW), part of the Great Sumatran Fault network.

decisive_move.sentence: The HypoDD relocation turned the BMKG catalogue's fixed-depth scatter into a ~20 km NW-SE band off all mapped faults, without which the Kajai Fault would not have been identified.

gates.evidence: The data are routine BMKG permanent-network arrivals and archived GSN teleseismic waveforms, collected whatever the hypothesis (p. 3-4). The new-fault claim could have failed if the relocated events had aligned with a mapped fault, and it faced checks (velocity-model swap, bootstrap, morphology, p. 5-6). The two stated rivals were never given separating predictions. HypoDD parameters were tuned by testing for the best results, and no analysis was fixed in advance (p. 3).

imports.item: Bootstrap resampling of residuals for location uncertainty (Efron 1982)
Simulated annealing search for the finite-fault source model

novelty_claims.quote: reveal a previously unknown ∼20 km long segment of the Sumatran Fault
A previously unidentified fault revealed by the February 25, 2022 (Mw 6.1) Pasaman Earthquake
[...] that it is a newly identified segment, which we call the Kajai Fault

limits: The XML text holds only the abstract and captions, so body steps are coded from PDF pages. The supplement (Figs. S1-S8) was not supplied; the residual decrease, velocity-model test, morphology support and filter-band test are coded from the authors' descriptions only. The two opening rivals are never given distinct predictions: the conclusion 'part of the Great Sumatran Fault network' and the 'conjugate fault' reading (p. 7) sit side by side unresolved, so the headline status is best_explanation. The HypoDD parameters are said to be stable 'over a reasonable range', but those runs are not shown. The rupture-extent agreement with aftershocks is partly circular (inference), because the fault plane for the inversion was chosen from the aftershock distribution (p. 4, p. 7). Sub-claim statuses: rupture model (asperity 2-11 km, Mw 6.14, stress drop 1.9 MPa) is estimate_with_resolution, but no formal resolution test is given and the authors admit non-uniqueness without near-field or geodetic data (p. 8). Nucleation mechanism: no conclusion among the stated rivals (p. 8). Raised hazard on the Angkola and Sumpur faults: no conclusion, 'Further work is required' (p. 9). The paper was received 2 April 2022 and revised 20 October 2022, but no review file was supplied, so changes forced in review cannot be coded. The data availability statements conflict (Zenodo DOI versus 'on request', p. 9). The text calls the event the '2021 Pasaman earthquake' (p. 5), a slip.

disagreements.support: The relocated sequence lies between the mapped Talamau and Angkola faults, which implies an unmapped fault; surface morphology adds support.
disagreements.quote: It is clear that the relocated foreshock, mainshock, and aftershocks are not located on any previously identified fault

disagreements.target: Weller et al. (2012); Lange et al. (2018) temporary-array studies
disagreements.support: The fault lies inside their study area but went undiscussed, which the authors attribute to limited seismicity during the 2008-2009 deployment.
disagreements.quote: due limited seismic activity during its deployment period (2008–2009), the possible presence of the [...]

disagreements.support: Relocation resolves events the catalogue held at a fixed depth and lowers travel-time residuals; the IASP91 centroid may be mislocated in depth.
disagreements.quote: the events that had previously been held at a fixed depth are now satisfactorily relocated
